title: Races, deadlocks, and memory visibility
hook: A race happens when two threads read and write shared state without coordination. A deadlock happens when threads wait on each other forever. Memory visibility is whether one thread sees another thread's writes — the .NET memory model guarantees visibility after proper synchronization.

blocks.text: A data race: thread A and B both increment _count without synchronization — you lose updates. A deadlock: thread A holds lock1 waiting for lock2 while thread B holds lock2 waiting for lock1. Visibility: without lock or volatile, CPU caches may let one thread see stale values — though lock and Interlocked establish proper ordering in practice.

entries.plainDefinition: Outcome depends on unpredictable thread scheduling when shared state lacks synchronization.
entries.example: Two threads incrementing a counter without lock lose one increment.

entries.plainDefinition: Circular wait where each thread holds a resource another needs.
entries.example: A waits on B's lock while B waits on A's lock.

entries.plainDefinition: Rules for which writes one thread observes from another.
entries.example: Exiting a lock ensures subsequent reads see prior writes inside the lock.

blocks.text: RabbitMQ consumers on multiple threads sharing a non-thread-safe Dictionary corrupt internal buckets. Deadlocks under load freeze services — often from lock ordering bugs or locking then awaiting messaging I/O. ConfigureAwait(false) in libraries avoids deadlocks with UI SynchronizationContext; ASP.NET Core has no context but lock-order bugs remain.

blocks.title: Deadlock prevention
blocks.body: Acquire locks in a fixed global order. Never await while holding a lock. Use timeouts on WaitAsync when appropriate.

snippet.label: Lost update race
snippet.explanation: Read-modify-write without synchronization loses updates under parallel handlers.

snippet.label: Lock ordering deadlock
snippet.explanation: Consistent lock ordering prevents circular wait. Prefer one lock or concurrent collections instead.

snippet.label: Unsafe shared dictionary
snippet.explanation: Dictionary is not thread-safe for concurrent writes. Use ConcurrentDictionary or message passing.

snippet.label: Sync-over-async deadlock pattern
snippet.explanation: Classic deadlock under load: lock held while .Result blocks waiting for a continuation that needs the same pool thread.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Assuming Dictionary is safe because reads are common. Different lock order in two methods. Using .Result after locking — blocks pool threads and worsens deadlocks.

blocks.text: How to prove it in production: data races corrupt in-memory structures silently — no exception, wrong counts in metrics. Capture thread dumps during a freeze (dotnet-dump collect) and look for threads blocked on Monitor.Wait or Task.Wait — circular waits indicate deadlock. The .NET memory model guarantees visibility after lock release, Interlocked operations, and volatile reads/writes. Without them, CPU reordering and cache lines can expose torn reads. Prefer eliminating shared mutable state (Channels) over proving correctness with fences.

blocks.title: Tradeoffs at senior level
rows: Fixed lock order; never .Result inside lock
Stress test + ThreadPool logging under load

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Saying races only happen on multi-core — even time-sliced threads on one core interleave. Claiming try/catch fixes races — exceptions do not fire on lost updates. Blaming ConfigureAwait(false) for all deadlocks without mentioning lock ordering or .Result. Insisting Dictionary is fine if you 'mostly read' — concurrent writes corrupt internal buckets.

interviewTakeaways: A data race is unsynchronized concurrent access where at least one side writes; deadlocks are circular waits — often from inconsistent lock order or sync-over-async.
The .NET memory model publishes writes after lock exit and Interlocked; without synchronization, visibility and atomicity are not guaranteed.
In production, capture dotnet-dump thread stacks when the service freezes — blocked Monitor.Wait chains reveal deadlock; metric drift without exceptions suggests races.

60s: Races need shared mutable state without coordination. Fix with Interlocked, lock, or message passing. Deadlocks need circular waits — use fixed lock order. Never .Result inside lock. ConcurrentDictionary beats locked Dictionary.
Follow-up: how does the thread pool make sync-over-async deadlocks more likely under load?
commonPitfalls: Saying 'my code is single-threaded enough' on ASP.NET Core gets you rejected — requests run on different pool threads concurrently.
Inconsistent lock acquisition order across two methods that take two locks.
Strong answer: 'Eliminate shared state with Channels. Fixed lock order when unavoidable. dotnet-dump for deadlocks. Interlocked for counters.'

jsTsCorrelations.note: JS avoids many races on the main thread but worker_threads and Atomics introduce the same concerns as C#.
Awaiting inside a synchronous mutex callback in workers mirrors .Result inside lock — the waiter blocks the thread the continuation needs.
